transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-22
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Ethan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Lucas (CSM); Karen (Halcyon Head of ML), Raj (Infra), Sofia (PM), Omar (Security)

Summary (auto):
Redwood and Halcyon scoping a 4-week POC to validate latency/throughput and cost for an LLM-based conversational assistant embedded in banking portals. Primary focus: workload characterization (QPS, concurrency), input/output token distribution, success criteria (latency, accuracy, cost), security constraints (VPC, KMS, audit logs).

Topics: POC success criteria, traffic profile, sizing, benchmark scenarios, timelines, security/compliance questions, next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Ethan: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro, im ethan park, account exec, and maya singh from our infra/se team is here to run through the workload modelling.
[00:18] Karen: hi all, thanks. im karen, head of ml at halcyon, excited to dig in. we want to make sure we scope the poc so it's realistic, and that we test both chat and transactional prompts.
[00:30] Maya: awesome. i can kick off with the high-level ask — what are your target qps and peak concurrency, and what token distributions you see? even ballparks help a ton.
[00:40] Sofia: for the pilot area (customer support + account help flows) we expect steady 30 qps during business hours, spiking to 120 qps for big events. concurrency per model instance about 20-30 requests at once, but overall concurrency across service could be 150 active sessions.
[01:05] Raj: to add, our current infra backs about 150 req/s at peak for microservices, but the LLM calls we intend to route to a dedicated inference tier. need VPC peering and strict egress controls.
[01:20] Maya: good, that's helpful. rough token sizes? average user prompt length and expected model output?
[01:28] Karen: typical user prompts are short, like 20-60 tokens, average ~40. responses vary — simple answers 30-80 tokens, complex flows (statement summaries, dispute explanation) can be 200-400 tokens. overall median output ~120 tokens, 95th ~320 tokens.
[01:50] Ethan: perfect — so for modelling let's use three buckets: small (in 20/30 out 40), medium (60 in 120 out), large (40 in 300 out) with relative frequency 60/30/10. does that reflect reality?
[02:05] Karen: yes that's close. maybe adjust to 65/25/10 but good enough for initial sizing.
[02:12] Maya: noted. next, success criteria for the POC — what does halcyon want as pass/fail?
[02:20] Sofia: two main things: latency and accuracy/usability. Latency: multimodal? No — text only for now. Targets: p50 below 400 ms and p95 under 1.2 s for the small/medium buckets when routed to dedicated capacity. For large responses 95th under 2.5 s is acceptable.
[02:40] Omar: security criteria: SOC2 equivalent controls, KMS integration for key management, audit logs for every request, and SSO (SAML/Okta). we will need documentation for data retention and encryption in transit+at rest.
[02:55] Ethan: yep we have SOC2 docs, KMS integrations, and audit trail exports. we'll share the security pack.
[03:00] Raj: on networking, do you support private deployment vs hosted calls? we prefer private (VPC) for phase 1, but can evaluate hosted with VPC peering if necessary.
[03:10] Maya: we support both. private deployment runs the control plane in your VPC with customer-managed subnets, and we can do on-prem variant if required. for the POC we usually start with a dedicated hosted instance with strict VPC peering and egress allow-listing to speed ramp.
[03:30] Sofia: timeline expectation? we want the POC to be short — 4 weeks ideally.
[03:34] Ethan: our standard 4-week pilot covers integration, benchmarks, and a light production simulation. we can define week 0 (kickoff + data exchange), week 1 bench setup, week 2 run scale tests, week 3 tune/optimize and collect SLO metrics, week 4 review and decision.
[03:55] Maya: for the workload modelling i want to propose a matrix: qps scenarios [10, 30, 60, 120], concurrency tests [10, 50, 150], token buckets small/medium/large as above, and model variants — base open model and quantized 8-bit variant. we'll run both latency and cost per 1k tokens.
[04:20] Karen: we need to compare cost to our current system too — current average cost is effectively $0.015 per inference (including infra) for short responses; if you can show a 2-3x cost improvement that's strong.
[04:35] Maya: noted. we'll compute cost per 1k input+output tokens for each model path and include batching effects. also include caching: prefix caching and KV cache can reduce repeated token generation for conversational state.
[04:55] Raj: how does continuous batching affect latency for small requests? our concern is tail latency when batching tries to aggregate small requests.
[05:04] Maya: we use workload-aware batching with latency SLO preservation — dynamic batch size with max delay thresholds. we'll include experiments with batch windows of 5, 10, 30 ms to show p95 tradeoffs. there will be cases where dedicated low-batch mode is better for p95 at higher cost.
[05:22] Ethan: also worth noting smart routing — if you want cheaper instances for background requests we can route non-critical traffic to lower-cost model variants automatically.
[05:31] Sofia: okay can you capture endpoint throughput per GPU for the model variants? we currently have a perf spreadsheet for our existing models but not for open LLMs.
[05:42] Maya: yes i will provide a table in the benchmark results: tokens/sec per GPU, avg latency, memory footprint, and recommended instance sizes. we'll also include a guidance sheet: how many GPUs for target steady qps and peak QPS with headroom.
[05:58] Karen: quick question on telemetry — we need token-level cost and latency attribution per customer and per route. can you do per-route dashboards?
[06:08] Lucas: yep our console gives per-route/model dashboards, token-level breakdown, and traces. retention tiers are configurable for audit needs.
[06:15] Omar: on compliance, we may ask for an on-prem or air-gapped option later — any blockers there?
[06:22] Maya: no blockers, on-prem package exists but it's heavier. for the POC we'll aim hosted/dedicated with VPC controls; we can scope air-gapped later if pilot goes well.
[06:30] Karen: for the benchmark inputs we'll provide 200 representative prompts across the 3 buckets, plus 7 long-form templates for the large bucket. expect a lot of banking jargon, names, and redactions.
[06:43] Maya: perfect — would you be able to include real tokenization artifacts? sometimes token counts change by tokenizer.
[06:50] Karen: yes i'll include both raw text and tokenized counts from our current tokenizer.
[06:55] Ethan: okay let's talk about the actual pass criteria to avoid ambiguity:
[07:00] Sofia: goal is: 1) p95 latency per bucket as specified earlier, 2) semantic accuracy on a held-out eval >= 92% (we'll define metric — intent accuracy + helpfulness judged by product), 3) cost per 1k tokens under $X (tbd), and 4) security controls verified (audit logs, KMS, SSO).
[07:20] Maya: for accuracy we recommend a small eval harness — 500 queries with expected outputs and a manual review for some. we can instrument automatic BLEU/ROUGE-ish metrics but human judgment will be used for policy tasks.
[07:34] Raj: for the infrastructure estimate — given your 30 qps steady and 120 peak with token medians, what do you think GPUs required?
[07:42] Maya: rough calc: small/medium/large mix and median tokens ~120 output + ~40 input average total 160 tokens. let's assume model throughput of 6 tokens/sec per T4-like GPU for a typical quantized 16-bit footprint — that would give roughly 960 tokens/sec per GPU, which is about 6 req/sec at 160 tokens per request. for 30 qps steady you'd need 5 GPUs minimum with headroom; for 120 peak you'd need 20 GPUs. but these numbers vary heavily with model choice and kernels; we'll provide exacts after running the specific models.
[08:15] Karen: those are higher than we'd hoped — any optimizations?
[08:18] Maya: yes quantization to int8 and kernel selection can push tokens/sec up by 2-4x depending on model. also batching increases tokens/sec per GPU but adds latency. KV/prefix caching can reduce repeated generation for conversational state massively for some flows (up to 60% token reduction in chat sessions).
[08:36] Ethan: also model distillation or a smaller instruction-tuned model for transactional tasks could lower footprint. we can recommend mixed-model routing: small model for transactional, bigger for summarization.
[08:47] Sofia: that mixed routing is interesting — we'd likely accept slightly lower fidelity for balance checks but want high fidelity for statement generation.
[08:56] Omar: security again — we need encryption at rest for caches and tokenized payloads. does your KV-cache support envelope encryption with a customer KMS?
[09:04] Maya: yes, we support KMS integrations and can encrypt KV caches with customer keys. we'll document key rotation and access controls.
[09:12] Raj: network egress — what ip ranges do you need? we have strict allow-lists.
[09:17] Ethan: we'll provide the egress CIDR and endpoints for the dedicated/hosted instance; for private deployment there's no public egress except management plane.
[09:26] Sofia: any blockers regarding regulators / data residency? we operate in EU and US regions, will probably require EU data residency for some customers.
[09:33] Maya: we can run the POC in eu-west if needed. need to confirm legal paperwork but we support region pinning.
[09:40] Karen: on the benchmarks, can we also simulate conversational sessions (multi-turn) to exercise KV cache?
[09:47] Maya: absolutely — we'll run a multi-turn simulation with 5-turn and 10-turn sessions and measure token re-use and effective token reduction with KV cache enabled vs disabled.
[09:56] Ethan: we'll include a cost model: per 1k token cost, GPU-run cost, and an expected monthly bill for production at your steady qps and peak assumptions.
[10:06] Sofia: perfect. any other blockers?
[10:10] Omar: one more from security — need to validate that audit logs are tamper-evident and can be exported to our SIEM.
[10:17] Lucas: logs can be streamed to your SIEM via syslog/s3 and include HMAC signatures; we'll include details in the security pack.
[10:24] -- (discussion continues with minor clarifications and a couple interruptions, some transcription noise) --
[25:12] Karen: so recapping: halcyon provides traffic sample and prompts; redwood runs the benchmark matrix and returns raw numbers + recommended GPU counts and cost modeling; both sides align on security docs; decision meeting in week 4.
[25:30] Ethan: yep i'll send the SOW and pricing and schedule the deep technical VPC review.
[25:36] Sofia: can you please include quick-run numbers for an 8-week pilot if we want to pilot larger scale?
[25:42] Maya: yes we can model both 4-week and 8-week pilots with different throughput targets.
[25:50] Karen: timeline wise we need the benchmarks and results before the end of march to decide for an april rollout.
[25:58] Ethan: we'll aim to share initial benchmarks by 2026-03-26.
[26:03] Raj: last quick thing — do you have a recommended visibility into queuing and backpressure? we want to instrument upstream for graceful degradation.
[26:12] Maya: we'll enable tracing hooks and backpressure signals (503s with retry-after) and configure autoscaling policies with SLO-aware fallback to cheaper models.
[26:23] Omar: thanks all.
[26:25] Ethan: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts and next meeting.

(roughly consistent with 58 minutes; remainder of call was Q&A and scheduling; the above captures the main decisions and artefacts requested)
